rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Anfāl comes from the reference to spoils in 8:1.
rows.anchor: takes its name from the reference to spoils in v. 1

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah 8 is early Madinan, although commentators assign some verses to the Makkan period.
rows.anchor: It is an early Madinan sūrah

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl maintains that 8:30 is Makkan, understood as referring to Quraysh's pre-Migration attempts on the Prophet's life.
rows.anchor: some maintain that v. 30 (Āl) is

rows.speaker: IJ, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: IJ, Q, and Ṭs hold that 8:30–36 are Makkan, in connection with Quraysh's pre-Migration attempts on the Prophet's life.
rows.anchor: vv. 30–36 (IJ, Q, Ṭs) are from the Makkan period

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl reports 8:63 as Makkan and revealed when ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb embraced Islam.
rows.anchor: v. 63 is Makkan, since it is reported to have been revealed when ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb embraced Islam (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah centers on Badr (624 CE), the first major Muslim–Quraysh battle, fought a year after the Migration amid Quraysh's continuing hostility.
rows.anchor: Battle of Badr (2/624), fought a year after the hijrah (the migration from Makkah to Madinah), the first major military confrontation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah addresses the fair distribution of war spoils, an issue absent when Muslims were an oppressed minority in Makkah.
rows.anchor: the matter of the spoils of war and their just distribution (vv. 1, 41)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah describes angelic aid in battle and God's will as determining victory.
rows.anchor: assistance of angels (vv. 9, 12) and the Will of God in determining victory, as in the famous statement from v. 17

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah treats battle's trials and the sincere believers' victory against great odds.
rows.anchor: challenges and trials of battle (vv. 10–11, 43–46) and the triumph of the sincere believers over great odds (vv. 65–66)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah gives guidelines for treating captives and observing treaties.
rows.anchor: guidelines for dealing with captives (vv. 67–70) as well as the observation of treaties (vv. 56–59)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Badr was an important first Muslim-community victory and is cited in Qurʾānic commentary as evidence of God's favor.
rows.anchor: The Battle of Badr was an important first victory for the young Muslim community and is cited in the commentary on many verses in the Quran as evidence of God’s Favor upon it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's final section outlines mutual responsibilities between Muslims who migrated to Madinah and those who remained behind.
rows.anchor: The last part of the sūrah addresses the relationship between those Muslims who had already migrated from Makkah to Madinah and those who had not, outlining their responsibilities toward one another

none: Qurʾān translation only; no commentary points.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plain sense is that God separates the bad from the good in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The plain sense would seem to point to this separation taking place in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The language recalls 3:179, which also speaks of God separating bad from good.
rows.anchor: Similar language is used in 3:179, which also speaks of God separating the bad from the good

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: IK allows that the separation may occur in this world, as at Uḥud when battle separated the Prophet's sincere followers from hypocrites.
rows.anchor: good and bad being separated from each other in this world (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name al-Tawbah derives from the sūrah's reference to repentance in 9:3.
rows.anchor: al-Tawbah, comes from the reference to repentance in v. 3

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Āl connects the name al-Tawbah to God's relenting toward the Prophet and believers in 9:117–118; the same verb is rendered repent or relent with different following prepositions.
rows.anchor: connect it with God’s“relenting” toward the Prophet and the believers as mentioned in vv. 117–18 (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾah, meaning “The Repudiation,” is another common name, taken from the first verse; commentators mention other names too.
rows.anchor: al-Barāʾah (“The Repudiation”), a word that appears in its first verse, and several other names are also mentioned by commentators

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Madinan sūrah opens with rules and political relations for fighting idolatrous Arabs and certain People of the Book, then criticizes corruption among religious leaders.
rows.anchor: how and why the believers should fight the idolatrous Arabs and also certain groups among the People of the Book (vv. 1–29), which is followed by a criticism of the corruption of religious leaders (vv. 29–32)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long passage recounts campaign-related trials and disagreements, including Madinan hypocrites' dissension over fighting alongside the Prophet.
rows.anchor: trials and disagreements that took place within the community over setting out on a military campaign and expands upon the dissension created by the hypocrites in Madinah who did not wish to go out to fight alongside the Prophet (vv. 38–106, 117–27)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah treats loyalty and allegiance through nomadic Arabs, hypocrites' rival mosque, and Muslims wavering in their commitment to follow the Prophet into battle.
rows.anchor: Loyalty and allegiance are major themes in the latter part of this sūrah and are applied to the attitudes of the nomadic Arabs (vv. 97–101), the efforts of some hypocrites to establish a competing mosque in Madinah (vv. 107–110), and the wavering and weakness of some Muslims in their commitment to following the Prophet into battle (vv. 117–18)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rules for zakāh and charitable giving are prominent themes.
rows.anchor: The rules governing the zakāh, or alms, and the giving of charity also figure prominently in this sūrah (vv. 58–60, 103–4)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah 9 is the only Qurʾānic sūrah that does not begin with the basmalah.
rows.anchor: the only sūrah of the Quran that does not begin with the basmalah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a report prompted by Ibn ʿAbbās's question, ʿAlī explains that the basmalah signals security, whereas this sūrah opens by severing a covenant and declaring conflict.
rows.anchor: He responded that the basmalah is a statement of security, and this sūrah begins with the severing of a covenant

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: Ali says that using the basmalah in letters inviting hostile groups to Islam is consistent: inviting people to God leads to peace, while rescinding a pact leads to war.
rows.anchor: this was precisely a call to God, not the rescinding of a pact; the former leads to peace, the latter to war

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Q notes a pre-Islamic custom of omitting the basmalah from a message that breaks a treaty.
rows.anchor: to omit In the Name of God in a message

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: R interprets the missing basmalah as reinforcing the link between the previous sūrah's closing verse about separation from disbelievers and this sūrah's opening message.
rows.anchor: the final verse of the previous sūrah, which emphasizes the need to separate from the disbelievers—a message given in a different form at the start of this sūrah (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Companions disagreed over whether Sūrahs 8 and 9 were one sūrah or two.
rows.anchor: it is recorded that there was disagreement among some of the Companions over this question

rows.speaker: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
rows.claim: An account attributed to ʿUmar says the Prophet directed sūrah and verse placement; because al-Tawbah was among the last revealed and seemed related to the previous sūrah, some Companions placed them together without a basmalah while unsure whether they were one or two.
rows.anchor: According to an account attributed to ʿUmar ibn

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some interpret the missing basmalah as preserving the Companions' difference of opinion over the arrangement of Sūrahs 8 and 9.
rows.anchor: some interpret the absence of the basmalah as preserving the difference of opinion

rows.speaker: traditional consensus
rows.claim: The consensus view is that the Prophet ordered the Qurʾānic sūrah arrangement and Sūrahs 8 and 9 are separate sūrahs.
rows.anchor: the traditional view accepted by consensus is that it was the Prophet himself
